name: EcoGiro
category: Inclusive recycling · Mobile UX · UX/UI Design
title: EcoGiro
summary: I turned recycling research into a collection MVP, connecting preparation guidance, citizen requests, and recycler responses.
audience: Citizens in Bogotá, recyclers, and collection centers.
problem: Citizens need guidance on preparing plastic. Recyclers receive mixed material and discover its condition at pickup. I focused the design on that gap: the information missing between preparation at home and collection.
question: How might we make preparing and handing over plastic simple for citizens, while giving recyclers the information and autonomy to collect it safely?
description: I designed the journey around a practical question: what does each person need to know before handing over plastic? Preparation guidance sits after the scan. Material details travel with the collection request so recyclers can review it before responding.
insight: Knowing the recycling rules does not ensure correct separation. Give material-specific instructions immediately after the scan.

process.title: Discovery
process.description: I structured the research questions and recycler interview guide, then synthesized the team’s interview and secondary research. Contamination and missing information became design priorities: preparation guidance after scanning and material details before pickup acceptance.

process.title: UX / Structure
process.description: I mapped the citizen, recycler, and collection-center journeys and defined the MVP sitemap. I separated sending a request from confirming collection and used Telegram as the proposed recycler channel. This gave the team a flow with explicit roles and response states.

process.title: UI Design
process.description: I translated the research into preparation guidance, a prominent scan action, and visible collection states. I documented recurring UI patterns so the same information and actions could stay consistent across screens.

process.title: Validation plan
process.description: I defined a pilot around the assumptions that could block the service: understanding the scan result, responding through Telegram, and completing a viable pickup. The plan tracks request completion, response time, material quality, and cost per kilogram.

architecture.description:
I organized the citizen app into Home, Collections, Rewards, and Profile. Scanning starts from Home and leads through preparation to a collection request. This keeps the main task in one flow and makes active requests easy to find.

I separated requesting a pickup from confirming one. Citizens propose an address and time; recyclers can accept, decline, or suggest another time through Telegram. The pending state makes clear that sending a request does not guarantee collection.

The service map connects citizens, EcoGiro, recyclers, and collection centers. I kept center-side material validation and centralized payments in the roadmap so the MVP could focus on preparation and coordination.

wireframes.description:
I gave scanning priority on Home and placed preparation guidance before scheduling. That sequence gives citizens the material information they need before committing to a collection request.

The wireframes keep the material summary visible while users enter collection details. I defined empty, pending, accepted, alternative-time, rejected, and collected states to cover the handoff beyond the ideal path.

screens.description: The MVP follows plastic from identification and preparation through the collection request and recycler response. I designed the supporting screens for profile details, contextual help, collection history, and reward progress around that journey.

designSystem.description: I brought the collection journey into a shared UI system with Poppins, Lucide React icons, and an 8-point spacing scale. The component specifications document dimensions and states for recurring actions such as scheduling, reviewing a request, and checking status.
designSystem.typography:
I used Poppins with distinct weights and sizes for screen titles, material instructions, actions, and supporting details. The hierarchy gives preparation steps priority over secondary information.

A clear hierarchy helps people scan material details and understand the next step without relying only on color or icons.
principles: Visible status with text and icons

closing.title: Outcome & Reflection
closing.description:
Across the two-month project, I connected research synthesis with user flows, the sitemap, and contextual education for the MVP. My contribution gave the team a design rationale for what information to show before a request and how to represent the recycler’s response.

The business proposal focused on collection centers as a potential B2B customer for coordination and traceability. I considered how pickup quantities, route density, and material quality would affect the experience. Pricing and operating costs still need validation.

The project reached an MVP and a pilot plan. The next step is to test it in a small area with a collection center and a limited recycler group. Usability, classification accuracy, and environmental impact have not yet been measured.
closing.credits: Five-person team · Two-month project. My contribution: UX research, insight synthesis, user flows, information architecture, contextual education, and product narrative.

tagline: Designing the connection between citizens and recyclers.
